title: The knives and the fruit
hookLine: the city's women, cutting fruit, see Yusuf and cut their hands

cards: Some things you can't keep inside a house. The Aziz told Yusuf to let the matter drop, but soon the city is talking. The Qur'an lets us hear the gossip.
Women of the city are saying: the Aziz's wife is chasing her young servant. He's struck her heart with love. We think she's clearly lost her way.
Gossip over dinner sounds much the same in any century. And she hears about it. She doesn't argue with the gossip.
She invites the gossips to dinner.

teach.h: A BANQUET, AND A KNIFE EACH.
teach.b: Surah Yusuf. She sends for them, prepares a banquet with cushions to recline on, and hands each of them a knife. Then she tells Yusuf: come out to them.
When they see him, they're so struck that they cut their own hands. They say: Allah preserve us!
This is no human being. This is nothing but a noble angel. And she says: there.
That's the one you blamed me for. Now, the fruit.
The title says fruit, and that's how the story is usually pictured, women peeling something when he walks in. But the Qur'an doesn't mention fruit at all, only a banquet and knives.
The fruit comes from the commentators, who wondered what the knives were for. Some said citrons; some said other things. The text is silent, and the image stuck anyway.
The gossips' word for her love is worth a look too: shaghafaha hubban. Commentators explain shaghaf as the thin covering around the heart. Love had gone right through it.
And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, describing his night journey in a hadith in Sahih Muslim, said he met Yusuf, who had been given half of beauty.
So this story takes beauty seriously. It isn't sinful to be beautiful, and Yusuf did nothing here but walk into a room. But beauty tested everyone in it.
The women who mocked, then couldn't hold a knife steady. The wife, who stopped hiding what she felt. And Yusuf, who is about to discover that being admired can be its own kind of trap.

how: Muslims describe Yusuf as having been given great beauty, citing the hadith of the night journey, and read the banquet scene as a reminder that beauty, like wealth or power, is a trust and a test.

o: a hot jealousy toward a rival in love
the gossip that spreads through a city
the thin covering around the heart

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the Qur'an says the women were cutting fruit
it mentions a banquet and knives. the fruit comes from the commentators.
a hadith says Yusuf was given half of beauty
the Prophet ﷺ said so, describing his night journey, in Sahih Muslim.
the story treats Yusuf's beauty as his sin
he only walked into a room. the beauty tested everyone in it.

games.q: you're the Aziz's wife. the whole city is gossiping about you. what do you do?
o: stay home until the talk dies down.
invite the gossips to a banquet, and call Yusuf in.
send Yusuf away to stop the rumors.
games.why: she hands each guest a knife and calls him out. they cut their hands and say: this is no human being. she says: that's the one you blamed me for.

practice: Think of the last time something striking caught your eye, a face, a sunset, a perfect car, and let your reaction come back: attraction, envy, the urge to take a photo, to own it, to compare yourself.
Look at it with curiosity, not shame, and then at how you feel about your own looks, anxious, proud, invisible. If you pray, you can ask for eyes that see beauty without being ruled by it.

wordCard.voice: Shaghaf, the covering around the heart: what love went through, the gossips said, when they saw Yusuf and cut their own hands.

orig.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 12:30: "he has struck her heart with love" — shaghaf, the covering around the heart.

carryVoice: Your line: beauty is a test too. Even the gossips couldn't hold a knife steady. Day sixty-two, done.
